GST billing

The tax decided by the rule, not by the typist.

Billing for distributors and traders where the software works out the GST instead of asking a person to pick it: place of supply decides IGST or CGST plus SGST, rates come from dated periods against the HSN or SAC code, and reverse charge and blocked credit ride on the line rather than in somebody's memory. Three things it does not do, said now rather than on call four: no IRN generation, no filing, and e-way bill numbers are recorded rather than raised.

Six decisions the invoice makes without asking

Each one is a place where a person choosing from a dropdown eventually chooses wrong, and the document still looks perfect.

  • Which tax, from place of supply

    Derived from the supply and recorded with the sub-section it came from, not read off the billing address. The total is identical either way, which is why the error survives so long.

  • Which rate, from a dated period

    Rates are held as periods against each HSN or SAC code. An invoice dated in March keeps March's rate for ever, including on a credit note raised in September.

  • Rounding, per line then totalled

    Each line rounds and the legs are added. Back-solving CGST and SGST out of a rounded total is how a split ends up a paisa short and a return refuses to reconcile.

  • Whether the GSTIN is real

    Fifteen characters ending in a checksum that either computes or does not. A wrong one blocks your customer's credit, and they find out at their month-end rather than yours.

  • Whether the buyer pays instead

    Reverse charge is a flag on the line. It suppresses the tax on the face of the document and prints the declaration the invoice rules require.

  • Whether the credit was ever claimable

    Blocked heads under Section 17(5) are decided line by line and shown beside the claimable figure, never netted off, because a netted number cannot be defended.

Place of supply, with the case that catches everyone

A Delhi wholesaler takes an order from a buyer registered in Maharashtra, who asks for delivery to their own client's site in Haryana. Sales looks at the customer record, sees Maharashtra, raises IGST. Right answer, wrong reason — and the same instinct on a Delhi-billed, Delhi-delivered order gets it wrong. In a bill-to ship-to supply the place of supply follows the third person who directed the delivery, and it stops depending on where the truck actually went.

The expensive version is quieter. Same document, correct total to the paisa, wrong head. Your buyer's credit lands in a pool they cannot use. Fixing it means a credit note and a fresh invoice, and if they already claimed it, a reversal with interest they will want from you. Nothing on the original invoice ever looked wrong, which is why it is usually found by somebody else's auditor.

So it is derived rather than chosen, with the rule kept on the document. Anything attached to immovable property follows the property, which is why a Mumbai company billing a Pune site's works contract to a Bengaluru buyer charges CGST and SGST. An engine answering from the customer master gets that wrong every single time.

HSN, SAC, and why a rate change never rewrites history

The most common data problem we find in existing billing tools: one rate field per item, overwritten whenever the rate moves.

  • Rates live as dated periods against the code. Change one on the twenty-second and invoices from the first to the twenty-first keep the old rate, with nobody editing anything.
  • A credit note reads the rate of the invoice it cancels, not today's rate. The opposite behaviour quietly creates a tax difference on every return in a year where a rate moved.
  • How many HSN digits you print depends on turnover. Above 5 crore it is six on business-to-business documents, below it four. A code valid at four can be short at six, and the invoice should be refused rather than rejected later by your buyer's portal.
  • A trader who also bills freight is running SAC codes alongside HSN, and mixing them is how a service line ends up at a goods rate.

One order, from quote to ledger

Nothing is typed twice, and each step freezes something.

  1. The quote

    Built against real items at real prices, with tax computed rather than entered. The argument three weeks later is about commercial terms, not about the total.

  2. The order

    Acceptance freezes the lines and pins the rates. No screen after this recomputes tax, because a screen that recomputes can disagree with the paper your customer is holding.

  3. The dispatch

    A challan against specific order lines with carrier, vehicle and driver, plus the e-way bill number and date where one is needed. Over-dispatch is refused by the database, naming the line and the outstanding quantity.

  4. The invoice and the registers

    Raised from what actually left the godown, in a numbering series checked for the collisions that break a portal upload. It lands in the sales register in the shape GSTR-1 wants, and exports to Tally with an identifier that updates on a re-run rather than duplicating.

Reverse charge, and the bills that show no tax at all

The easiest liability in Indian GST to miss, because the supplier's document gives you nothing to notice.

  • Goods transport, legal services from an advocate, sponsorship, imported services and specified purchases from unregistered suppliers put the tax on you rather than on the person billing you.
  • The flag drives both sides: the liability you owe and the credit you may claim, which are not always in the same period.
  • It is paid in cash, not out of your credit balance, which surprises anyone budgeting a heavy freight month from the credit ledger.

Questions people actually ask

We already bill in Tally or a small billing tool. Why change?

If your invoices are correct and nobody reconciles anything by hand, do not change. Distributors move for what surrounds the invoice: it is the last step of an order they could not see, against stock they could not promise, with credit nobody checked against 2B.

We have three GST registrations across states.

Several registrations in one workspace is normal, with the right one selected by the supply. Consolidating separate legal entities into one set of books is not something we do.

Our turnover crossed the e-invoicing threshold.

Raise it in the first conversation, because it changes the shape of the scope. You will keep generating IRNs the way you do today, and we will tell you honestly whether the rest is still worth it to you.

Send us three invoices that gave you trouble.

The one a customer's portal rejected, the one with a rate change in the middle of it, and the one nobody could explain. We will tell you which rule each broke.
